objective: Recommending and obtaining approval for a portfolio management reserve based on aggregate risk exposure
secondaryObjectives: Performing dependency analysis to identify and monitor risks across interdependent portfolio components
Maintaining a portfolio-level risk register tied to strategic goals and escalated component risks

sources.cite: PMI, Portfolio Management Professional (PfMP) Examination Content Outline (PRA-206-2017, July 2017): Strategic Alignment 25%, Governance 20%, Portfolio Performance 25%, Portfolio Risk Management 15%, Communications Management 15%
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of a copy of PMI's PDF hosted by a training provider. Relevant text: Strategic Alignment Task 5 scenarios 'in order to evaluate and select viable options'; Task 6 'Recommend portfolio scenario(s) and related components, based on prioritization analysis/criteria'; Task 7 'Determine the impact to portfolio and portfolio components due to changes in strategic goals and objectives'; Portfolio Performance Task 6 'Balance portfolio and prioritize portfolio components, using established criteria and methods'; Task 7 'Analyze and optimize the consolidated allocation/reallocation of capacity'; Governance Task 5 'Make recommendations and obtain approval regarding portfolio decisions'. Whether PMI has a newer outline was not checked. The objective wording is the course seed's. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's pfmp-water-utility-rebalance (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

The organization, the portfolio or program, the figures and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You manage the capital works portfolio of Eastmere City Council, a fictional council: 31 projects, 420 million dollars. Projects keep their own risk registers; there is no portfolio reserve.
handover: Three transport projects share one contractor and one road closure permit.
howItWorks: The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words and the docket.
Move on a fortnight at a time. A decision comes to you at each board meeting; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Meeting 2: the bridge repair slips; the permit window moves and the tram and depot both lose their slots.
Meeting 3: an escalated flooding risk to the depot is lost in email; it materializes in the autumn storms.
Meeting 4: the storm damage hits two projects at once; with no reserve, the council pauses the tram extension mid-build.

depPrompt.title: Risks that no single project sees
depPrompt.context: The shared contractor and permit link three projects.

choices.label: Register the shared-contractor and permit dependency as a portfolio risk with an owner, and monitor the three projects' milestones together

effects.log: A portfolio dependency risk is registered.

choices.feedback: Dependency analysis finds risks that exist only between components.

choices.label: Ask the three project managers to watch each other
Leave risk to the project registers
choices.feedback: The cascade isn't in any register.

regPrompt.title: A portfolio-level register
regPrompt.context: Project risks above thresholds are escalated by email.

choices.label: A portfolio risk register holding escalated component risks and portfolio risks, each linked to the strategic goal it threatens, reviewed at each board meeting

effects.log: The register links risks to goals.

choices.feedback: A portfolio register shows which strategic goals are exposed.

choices.label: Collect escalations in a spreadsheet
choices.feedback: A list, but no link to goals or review cadence.

resPrompt.title: No portfolio reserve
resPrompt.context: Aggregate exposure is about 35 million dollars.

choices.label: Recommend a 30 million dollar management reserve based on aggregate exposure and a Monte Carlo confidence of 80%, with release rules, for the board's approval

effects.log: The board approves the reserve and its rules.

choices.feedback: A portfolio reserve sized to aggregate exposure is cheaper than padding every project, and needs approval and rules.

choices.label: Ask each project to add 10% contingency
choices.feedback: Padding everywhere costs more and is spent locally.

choices.label: No reserve: projects have their own contingencies
choices.feedback: The cascade and portfolio risks have no funding when they hit.

reflection.question: Write the portfolio risk note for the board: what links the projects, what the register shows, and why the reserve is the size it is.

parts.label: Dependencies and register
parts.criteria: Shared contractor and permit as a portfolio risk; register tied to goals.
parts.modelAnswer: Three transport projects share a contractor and a permit; that dependency is a portfolio risk with an owner. The register links each risk to the goal it threatens.

parts.label: Reserve
parts.criteria: About 35 million dollars of aggregate exposure; 30 million at 80% confidence with release rules.
parts.modelAnswer: Aggregate exposure is about 35 million dollars; you approved a 30 million reserve at 80% confidence, released by the board's rules.

scoring.modelReasoning: Portfolio risk management looks between components: dependency analysis finds cascades no project register shows. A portfolio register holds escalated and portfolio risks tied to strategic goals. A management reserve sized to aggregate exposure, approved with release rules, covers portfolio risks more efficiently than padding each project.
